ταβέβλημαι, τοῦ Θεοῦ κατάλληλόν μοι φάρ μακον ἐπιθέντος.
english: The Lord says in the Gospels about those who make themselves dead to the world, whether they hand over their body to the stadium of martyrdom or to the labors of ascetic discipline, and in this way seem to lose and kill themselves by being deprived of the enjoyment of life: “Whoever has lost his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10:39). So for the one who is lost in this way, according to the Savior’s word, and finds his life, the prayer and the blessing are something great. Any person of sound mind would pray for this to come upon himself, and would say with understanding: “May the blessing of the one who is perishing come upon me” (Job 29:13).

“I was eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame” (Job 29:15). In a spiritual sense, he opened blind minds, and he helped those maimed in soul, and he himself became their eye. He gave feet to those lamed in the steps of the soul, and by his word he became their foot, and he led both by the hand. The eye is taken for intellectual guidance, and the foot for ethical guidance.
“I was a father to the powerless” (Job 29:16). In these words are shown the voices of one who helps the powerless, the weak.
“And I traced out a case I did not know” (Job 29:16). You see his protection: not only with money, not only with food and clothing, but even to the point of dangers I stood before another’s battle.

“And I shattered the jaws of the unjust” (Job 29:17). See the difficulty of the matter: as if from somewhere, he says, I set right a matter already seized in advance. Truly, when Christ came, he shattered the jaws of the opposing powers. The Lord shattered the jaws of the lions (Psalm 57:7 [58:6]), and it is written in the prophet: “I snatched the prey from their teeth.”

“And I said: My age will grow old like the trunk of a palm tree” (Job 29:18). See after how much time he says these things, not boasting, not being arrogant, but compelled to speak of God’s providence, and in what things he enjoyed it, and in what things he is now.

“But now the least of men have laughed at me; now they admonish me in turn, whose fathers I despised” (Job 30:1). He did not use contempt, but he knew them clearly, just as the prophet said: “Every evildoer is despised before him”; for he considered such people as nothing.

“And indeed the strength of their hands, what is it to me? Their end has perished upon them” (Job 30:2). “In want and famine, barren; those who fled yesterday into a waterless place, into distress and misery” (Job 30:3). From Olympiodorus, from Origen. But I did not ask for any help from them, he says, so that for this reason they would use such words against me. They long ago owed a penalty, being wicked, and in some way the punishment flew away from them. Or because they desired death because of extreme poverty, and did not obtain it, and were not made sober by their want to become parents of the good, but remained barren—those who yesterday, or a little before, had fled from the desert and from disasters. He seems to accuse them as ignoble, and as being from obscure places and poor fathers. “Their end has perished upon them” (Job 30:2): instead of, they never accomplished anything good.

“Those who circle around saltwort on the echoing place, whose food was saltwort” (Job 30:4). Saltwort is a certain plant, as they say, that quickly fills the one who eats it. “On the echoing place,” that is, on ravines and rocky places; for such places are resonant and echo back to those who speak. Or he calls the wooded place “echoing,” where the breath of the winds, moving the forest, produces a sound. So he says that these people wandered around the woods and the ravines and the places beside which flowing waters echo and murmur, because of extreme want, searching for plants and scraping the roots of trees for food as a consolation for hunger.
“Dishonored and despised, lacking every good thing” (Job 30:4). Another vice: to be such people even in poverty.
“For if only I could lay hands on myself” (Job 30:24). You see that “if I could” is not said because of weakness, but because of being prevented.
“And I stand crying out in the assembly” (Job 30:28). Because of the excess of his sufferings, he is not even ashamed before a crowd of people.

“I have become a brother of sirens, and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). I have fallen into the savagery of birds, he says; I have forgotten my own nature, and I am in no better condition than they are.

“For I stand in a just balance, and the Lord knows my innocence, if my foot has turned aside from the way” (Job 31:6–7). Ah, what precision! No one could say that because I used my wealth and former goods for idleness and dissipation, I am paying such a penalty and have been changed, with God applying a fitting remedy to me.
